payload.headline: Meta bounces 2.9%, but price still runs ahead of shrinking cash flow

summary.thesis: Meta's sales are still growing fast, but margins and free cash flow have fallen, and today's price assumes cash flow growth beyond what any of the valuation methods allow.
summary.decision: Long-term: wait. Swing: wait, because the price sits just under resistance with no room for a sensible target.
summary.act_at: Long-term near 475.85; swing only on a close above 663.81

payload.happening: META closed at 641.69, up 2.9% on the day. That puts it back inside the 636.45–644.84 zone, just above the 20-day average (637.06, falling) and below the 50-day average (679.7). There is no news since the last note, and the next earnings report is on 2027-01-27.
payload.business: Demand still looks solid. Trailing sales are 241.6B, up from 189.5B, a growth rate of 27.53%. Gross margin is 81.03%, so the core product is still very profitable to deliver. The real change is lower down. Quarterly growth slowed from 33.08% two quarters ago to 26.07%. Operating margin, the share of sales left after running costs, fell from 43.23% to 32.86%. Free cash flow, the cash left after investment, dropped from 44.8B to 28.6B, leaving an FCF margin of just 11.86%. The filings flag that profit per share is lagging sales and that the company missed forecasts last quarter by 29%. Both point to costs growing faster than revenue. The likely cause is heavy infrastructure and AI spending (general knowledge), but our data cannot confirm it. The balance sheet is not the issue: liquidity is 82.4B against 83.7B of debt, and share dilution is only 0.04%. The reported $14.2M of insider selling outside pre-set plans affects sentiment and governance, not the business. At risk: the margin and cash-flow recovery that the price depends on. Not at risk: demand, gross margin and short-term funding.

worth.text: There are two ways to value Meta, and they give very different answers. The cash-flow method (DCF) starts from today's 28.6B of free cash flow. It gives 248.92 in a bear case, 381.85 in a base case and 521.31 in a bull case, all well below 641.69. To justify today's price, free cash flow would have to start growing at 38.4% a year. That is above the 30% cap, which itself only gives 472.32. The sales-multiple method is kinder. Meta trades at 6.8 times sales, close to the peer median of 6.5, with a growth-adjusted ratio of 0.97, and at the 38th percentile of its own 5-year range. On its own history that implies 475.85 to 707.21, with 881.21 at the top. The gap comes down to one question: will margins return to normal? The sales multiple assumes they will. The DCF assumes the lower cash flow is here to stay. If the operating margin fell further to 24%, the value would be 242.33. The trailing P/E of 21.9 looks reasonable only because earnings have not yet felt the full hit from cash spending.
worth.key_assumption: Free cash flow recovers toward the earlier 44.8B as the spending pays off, instead of staying near 28.6B.

bull: Sales are still growing 27.53% over the trailing year, to 241.6B from 189.5B, a rare pace at this size.
Gross margin of 81.03% shows the core product is still highly profitable before investment spending.
At 6.8 times sales, Meta is near the peer median of 6.5 and at only the 38th percentile of its own 5-year range, and the own-history midpoint is 707.21.
bear: Free cash flow fell to 28.6B from 44.8B, and the price implies 38.4% starting cash-flow growth, above the 30% cap.
Operating margin dropped to 32.86% from 43.23%, and quarterly growth slowed to 26.07% from 33.08%.
Every DCF value, including the bull case of 521.31, sits below the 641.69 close, and a further margin slide to 24% points to 242.33.

levels.what: Bottom of the lower support zone (605.33–611.95). A close below it would break the trading range to the downside.
Low end of Meta's own price-to-sales history and close to the 472.32 DCF value at 30% growth. Here the case no longer depends on a full margin recovery.
Own-history midpoint. Above it, the price would assume the margin recovery has already happened.

longterm.why: The business is graded C, and the price is above every DCF value. Buying at 641.69 needs a cash-flow recovery the data does not yet show.

swing.why: The price is just under resistance at 651.93–663.81, which is less than one typical daily move (ATR 22.78) away, so there is no room for a sensible target versus a stop. The trend is a range below the 50-day average (679.7). Entry makes sense only on a close above 663.81, or on a hold of the 622.66–632.87 support zone (7 touches).

decision.timing: Options price about a 9.8% move by Dec 18 and 12.7% by Jan 15, both before the 2027-01-27 report. That report on margins and cash flow is the deciding event, so a long-term entry makes more sense after it.

change_mind: The 2027-01-27 report shows operating margin moving back toward 43.23% or free cash flow rising from 28.6B. That would support buying inside the 622.66–632.87 support zone.
The price reaches 475.85, where the own-history low and the 30%-growth DCF value (472.32) meet. That would justify a long-term buy even without a full recovery.
A close below 605.33 breaks the range lower and rules out any swing entry. A close above 681.33, together with a move back above the 50-day average (679.7), would turn the setup toward an entry.
payload.what_changed: Unchanged: still wait; the 2.9% bounce to 641.69 left the price above every DCF value (the top is 521.31), so the valuation gap that drove yesterday's wait is still there.
